pathway: Regular participation in 21st Century Community Learning Centers after-school programs (30 or more days a year) is associated with slightly fewer school-day absences than matched non-participants with similar prior-year attendance. Randomized trials have not shown that the programs cause this.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit. A program's own participant counts, a participants-only before-and-after change, or the federal measure of the share of students under 90 percent attendance who improved does not show this association.
typical_effect: Texas statewide: regular participants attended 0.3 to 1.4 percentage points more school days than matched non-participants (about 0.5 to 3.4 days a year, more at higher participation); two years at 60 or more days a year added about 1.1 to 1.2 points. New Jersey 2022-23: unexcused absence rate about 0.4 points lower (about three quarters of a day) than students who attended 15 days or fewer. Washington 2012-13: 14 percent (30 or more days) and 33 percent (60 or more days) fewer unexcused absences. Texas site-level study (779 centers): median center effect 0.14 standard deviations, with wide spread. Philadelphia (11 grantees): elementary regular participants were less likely to have 10 or more unexcused absences; no difference in middle or high school. Gains this size move the 90-percent share only for students close to the line.
caveats: Students who keep coming differ from those who do not, and matching on prior attendance handles this only in part. A meta-analysis of controlled studies of after-school programs for at-risk youth found a small, non-significant attendance effect, and randomized trials of middle school after-school programs and of After School Matters in Chicago found no attendance difference (see the row from P-02). Most state reports come from one evaluator (American Institutes for Research); the Texas site-level and Philadelphia studies are by other evaluators. New Jersey's 2022-23 comparison group is low-attending participants, not non-participants. Two arts-focused Philadelphia centers found no attendance difference. Test-score effects are near zero (L-12).
reason: Meets the research-associated bar only as rule 3 allows: matched comparisons that adjust for prior-year attendance in at least two independent state samples (Texas P-001/P-002, New Jersey P-005, Philadelphia P-089), all pointing the same way. Not tested: the causal evidence (P-009, P-010, P-011) is null. Checker figures used (participation bands are under 45 to 120 or more days, not 30/60/90/120; New Jersey compares with low attenders). P-013 dropped (UNSUPPORTED: the national evaluation's middle school comparison found fewer absences, so it cannot be cited as a null). P-008 (After School Matters, abstract only, another program) and P-012 (no attendance estimate confirmed) not needed.

pathway: Offering or attending a general after-school program did not reliably raise school-day attendance in randomized trials or in a meta-analysis of controlled studies, so after-school programs should not claim to raise attendance.
model_match: Not used for credit. Applies to general after-school programs, including 21st Century Community Learning Centers, After School Matters apprenticeships and middle school after-school programs.
typical_effect: Meta-analysis of after-school programs for at-risk youth (24 studies, 16 attendance estimates): small and not significant (a companion abstract reports 0.04 standard deviations, range minus 0.02 to 0.10). Randomized trials: no treatment-control difference in attendance for middle school programs (447 students), and no difference in days absent from transcripts for After School Matters (535 Chicago high school students). Pennsylvania 2023-24 state report: 66 percent of 7,149 participants at or below 90 percent prior-year attendance improved, with no comparison group.
caveats: Program attendance in the trials was often low. The Pennsylvania figure, and the federal measure it uses, reflect regression to the mean and never count as evidence. A review of five experimental after-school evaluations found 84 percent of 97 impacts not significant; its attendance estimate was not confirmed. The small adjusted association in state evaluations is recorded in L-44.
reason: Accepted as a do-not-claim row bounding L-44. P-013 dropped (UNSUPPORTED as a null). P-010 checked from its abstract only, so the Maryland location is not named. Y1.13 removed: an attendance-outcome statement does not describe the after-school model. Q-P03 merged here.

pathway: Personalized messages to families about their own child's absences (mailings, texts or teacher-written postcards) correct parents' underestimates, and their children then miss fewer days.
model_match: Repeated, personalized messages naming the child's own absences or missed learning, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. A single letter at the 90-percent line, a standard legalistic truancy notice or general family events do not qualify.
typical_effect: Texting trial in 4 urban districts (26,843 students, kindergarten to grade 5): chronic absence 2.4 to 3.6 percentage points lower from 20.5 percent (12 to 18 percent), 3.5 to 7.3 points lower for students with high prior absence, at about 6 to 9 dollars per student. 47 rural districts in 16 states: absences down 1.7 percent for the offer (about 0.2 days) and 4.5 percent for families reached (about half a day), at 4.07 dollars per student. Teacher postcards, preschool to grade 2: absences down 8.3 percent. Teacher-parent outreach in grades 1-2 in five schools: 5 to 6 points fewer students with 4 or more absences. Redesigned truancy notices: 0.07 fewer days absent than the standard notice.
caveats: Effects are small per student and smaller at scale. A single nudge letter at the 90-percent line had no overall effect (a middle school subgroup improved). Texts about grades and attendance in grades 6-11 in one Midwest district did not change chronic absence. Partners need record access through the school or district.
reason: Replication in a federal multi-district trial and a 47-district trial supports strong for the messaging model. P-029 dropped (UNSUPPORTED: the six-pilot report found a 6.8 percent family-engagement reduction, not a null). Checker figures used (P-015 from the working paper; P-016 includes preschool; P-019 is a comparison with the standard notice). P-020's home-visit component is unconfirmed, so only the text arm is cited. Cost range for the texting trial from the attendance-strategies thread (A-006).

pathway: Perfect-attendance awards did not raise later attendance, and awards given after the fact lowered it.
model_match: Not used for credit. A do-not-do entry for partner guidance and logic-model checks.
typical_effect: Pre-registered randomized field experiment, 15,329 students in grades 6-12 in 14 California districts: after-the-fact awards raised absences by 0.06 days in the target month (8.3 percent more); announced awards had no effect while in place and raised absences by 0.067 days after they ended.
caveats: One trial; it does not test recognition of improvement or group incentives.
reason: Checker confirmed design, population and direction. A2.5 dropped (a participation count does not describe an awards model).

pathway: A trained Check and Connect monitor who reviews each student's attendance records and follows up with the student and family cut absences for students in grades 5 to 7.
model_match: Check and Connect delivered with fidelity: a trained monitor assigned to each student, regular review of the student's attendance from school records, and structured follow-up with student and family, for students in grades 5 to 7. General mentoring does not qualify (see the row from P-06).
typical_effect: Chicago randomized trial (grades 1 to 8): students who took part in grades 5 to 7 had 4.2 fewer absences a year (22.9 percent); no detectable effect in grades 1 to 4; no effect on test scores or grades.
caveats: One trial, and the 4.2-day figure is the effect on students who took part, concentrated in one grade band. A Texas trial in middle and high schools, delivered by Communities In Schools and compared with its usual services, found no attendance effect, and a high school trial in a large urban district found no significant effects. The program cost about 1,700 dollars per participant a year.
reason: A large randomized trial with school-record outcomes of a model partners can run: suggestive. Not raised further because the older-grade replications were null; the Texas null used an active comparison (usual case management), so it is not a clean failed replication. Cost from the attendance-strategies thread (B-006). Two-year assignment not confirmed, so dropped from the model match.

pathway: School-based, community, peer and college-access mentoring, and mentors or facilitators assigned to off-track students, did not reliably change school-record attendance, course passing or high school completion in randomized trials and matched studies.
model_match: Not used for credit. Bounds L-25 (Success Mentors) and any mentoring logic model that claims attendance, on-track or graduation gains.
typical_effect: Federal Student Mentoring Program trial (2,573 students, grades 4-8): absenteeism 5.03 against 5.49 percent (effect size minus 0.09), not significant after correction for multiple tests. Peer Group Connection: 161.2 against 161.6 days (grade 6) and 166.3 against 165.7 days (grade 9). College-access mentoring (FLIGHT, Florida): effect size 0.01 on days absent. Achievement Mentoring (393 students, grades 10-11): 1.7 more days attended and 0.67 more credits, neither significant; suspensions 20 against 30 percent. Mentoring of off-track students in five districts and a facilitator program at two urban high schools: no significant effects on attendance, course passing, promotion or completion. School-based mentoring meta-analysis: effects very small and mostly not significant. Meta-analysis of randomized attendance trials: mentoring 0.63 days, with a range that includes zero.
caveats: Exceptions are listed separately: Check and Connect in grades 5 to 7 (P-05) and the education specialist for youth in foster care (P-07).
reason: Merged Q-P11, Q-P16 and Q-P43 (same studies or same model, indicators S3 and S4). P-029 dropped (UNSUPPORTED). Checker figures used: P-025 effect size minus 0.09 (not minus 0.05), P-031 0.02, Q-029 credits gain not significant (Q-P16 had said credits rose). Q-020 and P-028: Baltimore and the advocate role not confirmed, so described as a facilitator program at two urban high schools.

pathway: A dedicated education specialist who meets regularly with youth in foster care and works across school and child-welfare systems raised their school attendance.
model_match: The Fostering Opportunities model: an education specialist for youth in foster care in grades 6 to 12, with weekly check-ins and liaison with child-welfare caseworkers.
typical_effect: Colorado randomized trial (230 students in Jefferson County): attendance rate 7 percentage points higher at one year and 9 points at two years; clearinghouse effect size 0.49 (84 against 75 percent attendance in its 116-student sample).
caveats: One trial in one district; foster-care population only; the specialists were district staff in the trial.
reason: Randomized trial meeting clearinghouse standards without reservations, school-record outcome, model a partner could run: suggestive. F1.7 removed (a statement about families' knowledge of their rights does not describe a specialist model).

pathway: Weekly one-to-one play sessions with a trained paraprofessional for young children with low attendance and adjustment concerns were followed by higher attendance in one trial.
model_match: Not used for credit until replicated. Model checked: Primary Project (screened kindergarten to grade 2 students, trained child associates, weekly playroom sessions).
typical_effect: 249 students in seven schools of one northeastern city: attendance 87 against 84 percent (effect size 0.31); chronic absence 22 against 45 percent.
caveats: One compromised randomized trial (clearinghouse: meets standards with reservations); eligibility required both attendance below 90 percent and behavior concerns; developer-involved authors.
reason: This review holds tested-suggestive to one clean randomized trial or two independent strong quasi-experiments; a single compromised trial stays below. Population corrected per checker.

pathway: One-to-one literacy tutoring during the school day combined with a family engagement worker raised early-grade school attendance as well as reading.
model_match: The SPARK (Future Forward) model as tested: paid tutors give kindergarten to grade 2 students one-to-one literacy sessions several times a week during the school day for at least a full school year, plus a family engagement worker who contacts and visits each family regularly. Tutoring alone (L-05) or family engagement alone does not qualify.
typical_effect: Milwaukee two-year trial (576 students, seven schools): absences effect size 0.20, significant (clearinghouse), with a literacy effect of about 0.23. Earlier Milwaukee cohort (496 students, six schools): about 3.3 fewer absences, effect size 0.18, not significant. One-semester trial in Alabama and rural Wisconsin (127 students): no attendance effect.
caveats: Developer-led evaluations; only one of three trials found a significant attendance effect, and the shortest found none. Effect sizes for the significant trial come from clearinghouse summaries.
reason: One randomized trial meeting standards without reservations, with a same-direction earlier cohort; the null trial ran one semester of a multi-year model, so it is a weak replication test. Held at suggestive. F1.2 removed. P-037 place corrected (not Milwaukee). Weighed with PR-01, which uses the same trials for reading.

pathway: Daily math tutoring did not change total days absent in the larger Chicago trial; in the District of Columbia, students were less likely to be absent on the days they had tutoring.
typical_effect: Chicago first trial: plus 1.58 days absent (standard error 1.87), not significant. Earlier Chicago pilot of tutoring plus Becoming a Man (106 boys, one school): 10.3 fewer days absent for the offer, not significant after adjusting for multiple outcomes. District of Columbia tutoring initiative: 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on scheduled tutoring days (7 percent).
caveats: The District of Columbia estimate compares tutoring days with other days for the same students; no total or annual attendance effect was estimated, so it does not show a change in the 90-percent share. The Chicago pilot combined tutoring with a behavioral program.
reason: Not an overturn: the day-level design is weaker than the randomized null and the pilot result does not survive multiple-testing adjustment.

pathway: Summer programs that students return to over several summers, combining academics and enrichment, were followed by fewer school-year absences.
model_match: Multi-summer programs that students attend for two or more summers, combining academic and enrichment activities, with school-record attendance tracked (for example Horizons or Aim High). One-off camps do not qualify.
typical_effect: Aim High, San Francisco: unexcused absence rate about 1.06 percentage points lower three years after first participation; students attending all three summers 58 percent less likely to be chronically absent in grade 8. Horizons (1,324 students, 15 sites): attendance 95.8 against 94.6 percent (effect size 0.15); elementary 1.1 points higher (about two days); chronic absence not significantly different.
caveats: Two quasi-experiments, no randomized trial; students who return for more summers may differ from those who do not. A school-break science camp in Knox County, Tennessee did not change attendance. Aim High funded its evaluation under an independence agreement. Test-score effects of summer programs are small (L-07).
reason: Two independent strong quasi-experiments (within-student difference in differences; matched comparison with baseline equivalence) of the same model type: suggestive. P-042 dropped (UNSUPPORTED: the robotics program's attendance effect was positive, not null). A2.5 removed.

pathway: School-based telehealth clinics that let students be seen by a clinician during the school day cut absences and chronic absence.
model_match: The partner operates an on-site or telehealth clinic in the school that treats students during the school day. A nurse position alone, health education or health-system care coordination does not qualify.
typical_effect: Three rural North Carolina districts (staggered openings): chronic absence down 2.5 percentage points (29 percent) and about 0.8 fewer days absent (10 percent). Six elementary schools with telehealth (4,203 students, adjusting for prior absences): 7.7 percent fewer absences (0.6 days a year).
caveats: No randomized trial; rural and small-city settings. A full-time licensed practical nurse in elementary schools gave negligible or slightly worse attendance; a health-system care-coordination trial for children with chronic conditions found no attendance difference; school asthma education was null (L-66). A Hawai'i high school nurse program lowered chronic absence two to three years after adoption (size not checked), but it is a different model.
reason: Two independent quasi-experiments of telehealth clinics with school-record outcomes: suggestive; the nulls set the model-match boundary. A3.2 removed (a partnership statement does not describe running a clinic). P-045 kept only as a different-model note.

pathway: Online communities of practice for school licensed practical nurses focused on attendance lowered chronic absence in one trial; the version for registered nurses did not.
model_match: Not used for credit until replicated.
typical_effect: Cluster randomized trial in 84 urban elementary schools: significantly lower odds of chronic absence in schools whose licensed practical nurses joined (size not checked); no effect for registered nurses; about 764 to 896 dollars per school.
caveats: One district; the odds ratio was not checked; a partner's role would be facilitating district staff.
reason: Checker: the effect is in one arm only, which the proposal omitted. A single trial with one null arm stays below tested.

pathway: Paid community members stationed along routes to school at arrival and dismissal (Safe Passage) lowered school absence rates.
model_match: A community organization hires, trains and deploys adults on designated routes to school at arrival and dismissal times, as in Chicago's Safe Passage.
typical_effect: Chicago elementary schools (staggered rollout): absence rate down 0.58 percentage points (8.5 percent) in the published estimate; 0.78 points (11 percent) in the working paper. A separate study of the same program found violent crime down 14 percent and absenteeism down 2.5 points.
caveats: One city; school-level outcomes; both studies are quasi-experiments of the same program.
reason: P-050 PARTIAL: corrected citation is Komisarow and Gonzalez (2023), and the published 0.58 estimate is used. A second, independent study (McMillen, Sarmiento-Barbieri and Singh 2019) was checked in the attendance-strategies thread (E-029). Two independent strong quasi-experiments: suggestive.

pathway: Eligibility for a school bus or a full-fare transit pass raised attendance and cut chronic absence, while fare-free bus rides for students in one Florida county were followed by lower attendance.
model_match: Not used for credit: transportation eligibility is a district or transit-agency decision. Partners that help families use passes or routes may cite it only as context.
typical_effect: Michigan (walk-distance cutoffs, 50 largest districts): economically disadvantaged students' attendance up 0.5 to 1 percentage point and chronic absence down 2 to 4 points. New York City middle schools: a yellow bus or full-fare transit pass raised attendance 1.5 points (about 3 days). Leon County, Florida: fare-free rides for students went with lower attendance and more chronic absence.
caveats: The Florida study (synthetic control) was checked from its abstract only.
reason: P-053 corrected: authors Munoz and Sandoval (2022), and fare-free rides were for students, not all riders.

pathway: Changes to how or when school breakfast is served gave mixed attendance results: breakfast after the bell lowered chronic absence, while universal free breakfast and breakfast in the classroom did not change attendance.
model_match: Not used for credit: school meal policy, and Philadelphia already provides universal free meals.
typical_effect: Breakfast after the bell, Colorado and Nevada (regression discontinuity, 1,883 schools): chronic absence 8.9 against 16.9 percent (clearinghouse effect size 0.44). Federal universal free breakfast pilot (schools randomly assigned, six districts): no effect on attendance or tardiness. New York City breakfast in the classroom: no attendance effect. Philadelphia classroom breakfast trial (existing row): no attendance effect.
caveats: School meal policy, not partner programming.
reason: P-055 dropped (MISATTRIBUTED: two papers mixed, and the attendance result is unconfirmed). M-053 added from the math screener.

pathway: Housing subsidies and rapid rehousing for homeless families did not improve children's attendance, and rehousing families outside the city raised absences.
model_match: Not used for credit. If a partner rehouses families, keeping children in their school of origin with transport is the implied condition.
typical_effect: Randomized assignment of 172 students in homeless families in one city: children assigned to usual care did as well as or better than those assigned to housing interventions on attendance, mobility and achievement. One large urban district (within-student comparison): rapid rehousing and prevention lowered behavior incidents but raised absence and chronic absence, most for students rehoused outside the city.
caveats: One city each. The randomized study's link to a national housing trial and its use of school records were not confirmed.
reason: Replaces L-86's parent-report evidence with school-record studies.

pathway: Homelessness and eviction are associated with more school absences, and eviction itself causes more absences and school changes.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
typical_effect: Los Angeles (weighting on grade 3 attendance and math): homeless students missed 5.8 more days. Chicago and New York City (random assignment of eviction cases to judges): eviction raised the share of days absent by 2.4 percentage points (about 4.3 days) and chronic absence by 8.8 points, and increased school changes.
caveats: Programs that rehoused families did not raise attendance (L-86). The eviction study found little effect on grade 3 to 8 test scores, so no link to the grade 3 reading test is claimed and S5 is dropped from this row.
reason: Two independent studies, one adjusting for prior attendance and one causal, meet the associated bar. P-059 population corrected (Chicago and New York City).

pathway: Community schools that coordinate health, family and learning services on site cut chronic absence in New York City and California, but not in Tennessee.
model_match: Unchanged from L-36: the partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained at least three years.
typical_effect: New York City: chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 (high school), three-year average. California (matched schools, first full year): chronic absence fell 1.5 points more than in matched schools (about 30 percent more), 2.8 points in elementary schools. Tennessee (statewide, staggered adoption): chronic absence rose 1.3 points (5.9 percent). Plan on the California size, not the New York City size.
caveats: The Tennessee estimate is less certain because of pre-existing trends. Massachusetts Wraparound Zones, a lighter model, showed no attendance effect. Case management in Kalamazoo elementary schools improved attendance (size not checked), unlike the national case-management trial in L-41.
reason: Downgraded from B to suggestive: one at-scale positive (New York City), one first-year matched positive (California, 1.5 points absolute, not 30 percent), one statewide negative (Tennessee; also counter-evidence G-042 in the attendance-strategies thread). Not overturned, because two of three full community-school evaluations are positive and the negative has pre-trend concerns. Weighed with Q-P35 (dropout), M-P20 and M-P21 (math).

pathway: Whole-school restorative practices reduced suspensions but did not reliably change attendance or chronic absence.
typical_effect: Pittsburgh school-randomized trial (44 schools): 0.92 fewer days absent (effect size minus 0.065) and 2 points less chronic absence, neither significant. Saint Paul (7 schools against 14 matched): no attendance improvement. Restorative practices added to Diplomas Now (33 schools randomized): fewer suspensions of 3 or more days; chronic absence reduction only marginally significant.
caveats: Suspension effects are real and belong to other pathways. A clearinghouse rated the Pittsburgh student-level attendance estimate promising (0.07), but it was not significant in the trial.
reason: Checker figures used for Pittsburgh (effect size minus 0.065, student-level estimates). Clearinghouse rating from the attendance-strategies thread (G-032).

pathway: Court-based truancy diversion did not improve attendance once regression to the mean was accounted for.
model_match: Not used for credit. Also a methods warning: before-and-after gains for students chosen because of high absence are biased upward.
typical_effect: Elementary students in five Minnesota districts (difference in differences against non-implementing schools): no program effect. Grades 7-10 in a Midwest county (matched against a neighboring county): similar or slightly lower attendance, no consistent pattern.
caveats: A community-based truancy court in a large urban district had fewer unexcused absences after one year than traditional court, but groups were matched on demographics only, and the city and baseline absences were not confirmed.
reason: F1.7 replaced with Y8.13 (justice diversion), which describes the model.

pathway: A school early-warning and monitoring system cut chronic absence and course failure after one year in a United States trial, but a Norwegian trial found no effect on absence or completion, and no study measured graduation or dropout.
model_match: Not used for credit: a school or district system. Partners who use school data to target students can describe it as a practice, not as an effect on these indicators.
typical_effect: Midwest trial (73 high schools, 37,671 students): chronic absence 10 against 14 percent; course failure 21 against 26 percent; no effect on credits, low grade point average or suspension; dropout and graduation not examined. Norway (42 schools, 7,677 students): no significant effects on absence, completion or results after two years.
caveats: School-run; outcomes are one-year on-track steps.
reason: Merged Q-P15 (same system, S3 and S4).

pathway: A school-wide social and character curriculum (Positive Action) was followed by lower school-level absenteeism in two cluster trials, but clearinghouse reviews of the same trials disagree on whether the effect is significant.
model_match: Not used for credit until the conflict is resolved.
typical_effect: Hawai'i (20 elementary schools): authors report 15.2 percent lower absenteeism; clearinghouse found it not significant (10.0 against 11.6). Chicago (14 schools): authors report lower absenteeism; one clearinghouse review found it not significant (5.6 against 7.0); another review of a paper from the same trial found a significant positive effect.
caveats: School-level outcomes; developer-involved trials.
reason: Checker could not find the claimed effect size of 0.19; the 15.2 percent figure is used. M-066 adds the conflicting clearinghouse finding.

pathway: Playing on a school sports team is associated with fewer absences during the season, comparing each student with themselves.
model_match: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit. The studies cover school interscholastic teams, not community leagues.
typical_effect: Indiana (about 262,000 high school students, student fixed effects): absence rate 0.70 points lower in season (0.89 for team sports). Earlier study (existing row): unexcused absences declined for male athletes, partly offset the day after games.
caveats: Within-student designs control fixed traits but not season-specific motivation. The Indiana chronic-absence gap (10 against 23 percent) is descriptive. Transfer to partner sports programs is untested.
reason: Two independent within-student longitudinal studies meet the associated bar. The descriptive chronic-absence gap is not used as an effect.

pathway: Relationship-building teacher home visits were followed by slightly higher attendance and math scores in a matched study in the District of Columbia, but a St. Louis randomized trial found no differences.
typical_effect: District of Columbia, grades 1-5 (matched comparison): attendance 95.28 against 94.93 percent (effect size 0.07); grades 4-5 math 0.11 standard deviations higher on combined state tests; reading not significant. St. Louis (teachers randomized within 11 schools): chronic absence 0.3 points lower, not significant; no academic differences. Connecticut's Learner Engagement and Attendance Program: attendance about 4 points higher in the month after a first visit for chronically absent students.
caveats: Families who accept visits differ from those who do not. The Connecticut study compares students visited earlier with students visited later, without matching on prior attendance, and its visits re-engaged chronically absent students, a different model. A Washoe County evaluation found no relationship once prior-year risk was controlled. The St. Louis trial had fidelity problems.
reason: Merged M-P23 (math part). Washoe County result from the attendance-strategies thread (A-029). One matched positive and one randomized null stay below tested.

pathway: State human-services caseworkers placed in schools to help families with basic needs were followed by lower chronic absence.
model_match: Not used for credit: Michigan's Pathways to Potential is run by the state human-services agency, and the evidence is one study without comparison schools.
typical_effect: 160 Michigan schools (interrupted time series at staggered start dates): chronic absence about 8 percent lower (relative, not percentage points), about 21 students per school a year.
caveats: No comparison schools beyond staggered timing.
reason: Not a strong quasi-experiment and not a partner model. A3.2 removed.
P-080 is UNREACHABLE (also unreachable in the attendance-strategies thread, E-021). No source was fetched, so even a no-evidence row cannot state what the sponsor claimed.

pathway: Across many attendance interventions, average effects on attendance are small and vary widely by model.
model_match: Not used for credit; a magnitude benchmark for checking logic models, not a model.
typical_effect: 22 controlled United States studies to 2018: 0.25 standard deviations (range 0.14 to 0.36); the family-school partnership range includes zero. 13 United States studies from 2020 to 2025: 0.09. Meta-analysis of randomized trials (61 articles): parental engagement 0.43 more days (range 0.10 to 0.76). 49 United States school-based studies from 2016 to 2025 with school-record attendance: chronic absence minus 0.054 standard deviations overall, minus 0.107 for messages to parents, minus 0.073 for whole-school approaches. Indicated interventions for students already missing school: moderate positive effects with wide spread (pooled size not checked).
caveats: Pooled sizes mix models. The 49-study figures come from a summary, not the full report, and its categories are curriculum, mentoring, family connectedness, parent messaging and whole-school. A claimed attendance gain well above about 0.1 to 0.25 standard deviations should be questioned.
reason: P-084 corrected per checker (years 2016 to 2025; categories; transportation and breakfast not named). Y8.5 and A2.6 not used: the benchmark applies to any attendance claim.

pathway: Cash rewards to families tied to attendance, test scores and other activities did not raise attendance, test scores or graduation overall; welfare rules tying benefits to teen attendance raised some attendance measures but not completion.
model_match: Not used for credit. Models checked: Opportunity New York City Family Rewards, Family Rewards 2.0 (Bronx and Memphis), Ohio's welfare initiative for teen parents, and a San Diego welfare attendance rule.
typical_effect: Family Rewards (about 4,800 families): few effects for elementary and middle school students on attendance or tests; on-time graduation 49.2 against 48.2 percent overall; for ninth graders who were proficient readers, graduation up 8 points and 9.5 points more passed five or more Regents exams. Family Rewards 2.0: no effect on school progress through year 4 (on-time graduation 63.4 against 63.1). Ohio teen parents: high school or equivalency 34.0 against 31.9 percent, not significant. San Diego: more students met an 80 percent attendance rule; no difference in dropout or graduation.
caveats: Welfare sanctions are state policy, not partner programming.
reason: Merged Q-P27 and M-P17 (same F2.1 models across indicators). Q-049 is MISATTRIBUTED, but its corrected citation (Miller, Miller, Verma and others, 2016) says what the row needs. S10 not included: the Regents result spans subjects.

pathway: Admission to a career academy or technical high school reduced ninth-grade absences.
model_match: Not used for credit: school enrollment, not a partner program.
typical_effect: Wake County, North Carolina technology career academy (admission lottery): about 1.4 fewer ninth-grade absence days (38 percent of the control mean). Connecticut (existing row): attendance up 1.7 points for boys.
caveats: School model.
reason: Lottery evidence confirmed by the checker.

pathway: Longer exposure to whole-school inclusion programs (Special Olympics Unified Champion Schools) was followed by slightly lower absence for students with intellectual disabilities in grades 3 to 8 only.
typical_effect: North Carolina (11 years, difference in differences): each year of exposure lowered the absence rate 0.3 points for students with intellectual disabilities in grades 3-8; in high school, a 0.01-point drop for other students and none for students with intellectual disabilities.
caveats: Schools chose their exposure; effects are small and limited to one group and level.
reason: Checker: direction mixed by level. A single quasi-experiment with a subgroup effect stays below tested. Y8.2 removed.

pathway: Students who attend some multi-year after-school programs heavily and for several years drop out less and graduate on time more often than similar students, but the evidence comes mainly from one program and does not show the programs cause it.

pathway: Tutoring programs that build children's math skills raise scores on math tests, but at scale the gain on state tests is small or not detectable.
model_match: Tutoring by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as Math Corps), during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured math curriculum. typical_effect: Math Corps randomized trials: 0.17 (0.24 at intended dosage) and about 0.18 on broad math tests; the state test was not significantly different in the grades 4 to 8 and statewide trials. Plan on 0 to 0.10 on the state test.
caveats: Most gains are on non-state tests; the two Math Corps trials that used the state test found no significant difference.
reason: Merges M-P02 and M-P03. Downgraded from strong to good: replicated trials, but null on the state test at scale. M-003 not used (math part unconfirmed).

pathway: Universal social and emotional learning curricula taught during the school day raise students' test scores slightly, and the gain is smaller in the largest, most rigorous trials than in earlier reviews.
model_match: A universal, sequenced social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day by trained teachers or partner staff, for at least a full school year. After-school or pull-out social skills groups and one-off assemblies do not qualify.
typical_effect: Meta-analysis of school-based programs: overall 0.08 standard deviations (math 0.08, English 0.07), smaller in randomized trials than in quasi-experiments. Another meta-analysis: reading 0.25 and math 0.26, with smaller effects in large rigorous randomized trials. Positive Action in Chicago: the authors report a marginal math gain, the clearinghouse finds state reading and math not significant, and absenteeism improved. Positive Action in Hawaii: large gains per the authors, not significant in the clearinghouse review. INSIGHTS: early gains faded by middle school. A classroom social skills program: no main effects. Plan on 0.05 to 0.08 on state tests.
caveats: The federal seven-program social and emotional learning trial could not use test scores (it used rating scales), so it neither supports nor refutes this link. A science effect (0.06) rests on three estimates and is not added. Program developers ran several of the positive trials.
reason: Proposed as an overturn for math; not overturned because the best pooled estimate is still positive (0.08 for math).
